title: Submission, Status and Failure
subtitle: Queue, retry, adopt and poll: what happens between clicking submit and LHDN saying Valid
outcomes: Walk the full lifecycle from Sales Invoice submit to a Valid or Invalid verdict
Read every log status and know which ones need a human
Distinguish an accepted submission from a validated document
Diagnose rate limits, timeouts and authentication failures from the log alone
Recover safely from a lost response without creating a duplicate

slides.title: The lifecycle in one picture
bullets: Invoice submit queues a background job, which builds and validates the document locally
A log row is written before the HTTP call, so a crash still leaves evidence
LHDN answers 202 with a submission UID plus accepted and rejected document lists
Accepted documents then wait for asynchronous validation by a scheduled poll
The poll writes Valid or Invalid, with validation results, back to the log and the invoice

rows: Whether LHDN or the network is at fault

slides.notes: Draw this on a whiteboard if you can: one horizontal line, four checkpoints. The key teaching point is that acceptance and validation are different events separated by minutes or hours, which is why an accountant refreshing a form cannot tell whether a document is fine. Only the log knows the whole sequence.

slides.title: What each status means, and who acts
bullets: Queued and Retry are internal: the app still intends to submit
Submitted means LHDN accepted the document for processing, not that it is valid
Valid means validation passed and a UUID exists; this is the state you want everywhere
Invalid means LHDN processed it and found a problem; the validation results say what
Rejected means LHDN refused the document at intake, usually numbering or malformed data
Cancelled and Error close the loop: one is deliberate, the other needs investigation
slides.notes: Most support time is wasted because people cannot name the state they are looking at. Drill the difference between Submitted and Valid until it is automatic. Also make the point that Valid with a warning is still a valid document: warnings are for the month-end review, not for immediate panic.

slides.title: Accepted is not validated
bullets: The submission call returns a submission UID plus per-document outcomes
Rejection at this stage is about the envelope: duplicates, malformed JSON, unknown taxpayer
Acceptance only means LHDN has queued the document for validation
The scheduled poll runs every ten minutes and fetches document details by UUID
An Invalid verdict carries validation results that point at specific fields
slides.notes: This is the distinction that breaks dashboards. A naive report counting accepted submissions will overstate compliance, sometimes badly. Teach people to count Valid documents. If validation never arrives, the first suspect is the scheduler, the second is the token, and only the third is the app.

slides.title: Three families of failure and how each is handled
bullets: Transport problems: timeouts, 429 and 5xx are retried with exponential backoff honouring Retry-After
Authentication problems: one transparent token refresh, then an error that needs a human
Business problems: validation errors, duplicates and rejected documents need data changes, not retries
Retries are bounded by Max Retries, after which the row is marked Error and surfaced
Retry budget is deliberately small, because endless retries hide a systemic defect
slides.notes: Explain the difference between a transient fault and a permanent one, because retrying a permanent failure is how queues fill up and rate limits get worse. Retry-After is LHDN telling you when to come back, and honouring it is both polite and effective. When the retry budget is exhausted, the app marks the row rather than pretending.

slides.title: The lost response, and why it is the dangerous one
bullets: A network failure after LHDN accepted a document leaves you with no UUID and no error
The retry first searches LHDN by invoice number before submitting again
If the document exists, the app adopts it and records the UUID instead of duplicating
Before adoption existed, the standard failure was a duplicate invoice that could not be cancelled
Adoption depends on the invoice number being unique and meaningful, which is why naming series matter

callout.title: Never 'just resubmit'
callout.text: Resubmitting after a timeout is how duplicates are born. Refresh the log, let recovery search LHDN, and only submit again when the search is conclusive.

slides.notes: This is the most valuable operational slide in the course. Explain the sequence concretely: submit, LHDN accepts, the response is lost, the retry adopts. Then explain what to do if the adoption search is inconclusive: check the MyInvois portal by invoice number before forcing anything. Duplicate prevention is cheaper than duplicate cleanup, and cancellation windows make cleanup urgent.

slides.title: Duplicate invoice numbers and idempotency
bullets: LHDN enforces uniqueness on document numbers permanently, across all your submissions
A re-run of the same Sales Invoice is caught by the document hash on accepted log rows
A deliberately reissued invoice needs a new number, because it is genuinely a new document
Test environments that reuse production numbering create avoidable duplicates later
Keep the log forever: it is the only record of which numbers have been consumed
slides.notes: Idempotency here has two layers: a document hash guard inside the app, and an invoice-number uniqueness rule at LHDN. Explain that they protect different things, and that neither helps if a clerk manually creates a second invoice with the same number. The naming series conversation from chapter five comes back here with teeth.

slides.title: Watching the queue without watching it all day
bullets: Confirm the scheduler is enabled, otherwise nothing polls and everything looks stuck
Filter the log by status to build three views: needs attention, waiting, done
Alert on Error or Invalid rows older than a business day, not on every failure
Watch the attempts counter: rising attempts across many rows means an infrastructure fault
Review Submitted rows older than an hour before month-end close, not after
slides.notes: Monitoring should produce a small number of decisions, not a stream of notifications. Three saved filters cover most operations: everything waiting, everything broken, everything done today. The attempts counter is an underrated signal, because a single retry is noise while a hundred rows on their third attempt is an outage.

slides.title: A stuck invoice, step by step
bullets: Open the log row and read the error text before touching anything else
Check the stored request and response bodies to see what LHDN actually said
Refresh the status once, in case validation has completed since the last poll
If the status is Error with a transport message, let the retry job run before intervening
If the document was rejected for data, fix the master data and use resubmit
paths: E Invoice Submission Log → filter by Sales Invoice
Sales Invoice → Malaysia e-Invoice → e-Invoice Status → Refresh from MyInvois
Malaysia E-Invoice Settings → check Environment and credentials
slides.notes: A runbook beats intelligence under pressure. The order matters: read, verify, refresh, wait, fix. Skipping to 'fix' is what creates duplicates. Encourage teams to paste the log's error text into their ticket rather than a screenshot of the invoice, because the error is the diagnostic and the invoice is just the patient.

lab.title: Failure drills on sandbox
steps: Submit three clean invoices and watch each log row move from Queued to Submitted and then Valid
Deliberately remove an item's MSIC code and submit a fourth invoice to see local validation refuse it
Restore the code, submit, and confirm the new log row reaches Valid with a different hash
Break the client secret in settings, submit an invoice, and read the authentication error on the log
Restore the secret, run the status refresh, and confirm the queued document recovers
Force a duplicate by submitting the same Sales Invoice name again through the API and read the rejection
Open one log row and identify the request body, the response body, the UUID and the attempts counter
lab.done: You have four log rows covering Valid, blocked-by-validation, authentication failure and duplicate, and you can explain each status transition using only the fields on the log.

quiz.question: LHDN returns 202 with the document in acceptedDocuments. What is the status now?
quiz.why: Acceptance only queues the document. A UUID and a Valid verdict arrive later, when the scheduled poll fetches document details.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Invalid and Rejected?
options: Invalid failed validation after intake; Rejected was refused at intake, often for duplicates or a malformed envelope
Rejected means the buyer refused the invoice
quiz.why: Rejection happens at submission time, usually on numbering or payload structure. Invalid comes later from asynchronous validation and points at data.

quiz.question: A submission times out with no response. What should the app do on retry?
options: Submit again with a new invoice number
Search LHDN by invoice number and adopt the document if it exists
quiz.why: Lost-response recovery searches for the document first. Adopting an existing document avoids the duplicate that a blind resubmission would create.

quiz.question: LHDN answers 429 with a Retry-After header. What is correct behaviour?
options: Ignore the header and retry immediately
Back off for the interval LHDN specifies, then retry within the retry budget
Submit the rest of the batch faster to catch up
quiz.why: Retry-After is an instruction, not a suggestion. Honouring it avoids deepening the rate limit and is built into the client.

quiz.question: Every submitted invoice stays at Submitted for a day. What is the first thing to check?
options: Whether the site scheduler is running, since polling is a scheduled job
quiz.why: Validation status only advances when the poll runs. A disabled scheduler leaves every document at Submitted regardless of LHDN's verdict.

narration: Chapter six is what happens after you press submit. The invoice is queued as a background job, validated locally, written to a log row, and only then sent to LHDN. The submission call returns a submission UID with accepted and rejected documents, which is not the same as validation. Acceptance means LHDN has queued the document; a scheduled poll every ten minutes fetches the details and writes valid or invalid back to the log and the invoice. Learn the statuses: queued and retry are internal, submitted is waiting, valid is done, invalid needs data changes, rejected was refused at intake, cancelled is deliberate, error needs investigation. Failures come in three families. Transport problems like a timeout, a four two nine or a five hundred are retried with backoff that honours retry after. Authentication problems get one transparent refresh, then need a human. Business problems need the data fixed, not another attempt. The most dangerous failure is the lost response: LHDN accepted the document, the answer never arrived, and a naive retry creates a duplicate. The app searches by invoice number and adopts what it finds, so never just resubmit. Monitoring is three saved filters: waiting, broken, and done today. A stuck invoice has an order: read the error, read the request and response, refresh, let retry run, then fix. In the lab you break things on purpose.
